questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of a notice?
questions.answer:
**(A)** Salutation

A notice has the **name of the institution at the top, the word NOTICE, a date, a heading or subject, the body, and the signature with the designation**. A **salutation** ("Dear Sir", "Respected Madam") belongs to a letter; a notice is addressed to nobody in particular and everybody on the board at once.

questions.question: What is written at the top of a notice?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Name of institution

A notice is always issued in the name of a body — the school, the college, the office or the club — and that **name is written first, at the top, in capitals**. Only then come the word NOTICE, the date, the heading and the body. Without the institution's name the notice has no authority behind it.

questions.question: Which tense is commonly used in writing a report?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Past Tense

A report records an event that has **already happened**, so the narration is in the **past tense** ("The function began at 10 a.m.", "The Chief Guest inaugurated..."). Only the concluding sentence or a general observation may shift to the present.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Yours sincerely

The standard subscription of a formal letter is "**Yours sincerely**". "Your" is a possessive adjective and cannot stand alone as the close of a letter; "your's" is a wrong form, since **no possessive apostrophe is used with "yours"**. (*The solved booklet marks the third option; the correct form is the fourth.*)

questions.question: What is written at the top of an article?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Heading / Title

An article opens with a **heading or title**, with the writer's name below it, and then the body in paragraphs. A date, a salutation and a subscription are the furniture of letters and notices, not of an article.

questions.question: Where was the poet, Kamala Das, driving to?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Cochin airport

The poet is driving **from her parents' home to Cochin airport**, from where she is to fly away. Her mother dozes beside her in the car, and it is this last look at her — "ashen like that of a corpse" — that the poem records.

questions.question: According to the poet, a thing of beauty keeps us
questions.answer:
**(D)** Healthy and peaceful

Keats says that "a thing of beauty is a joy for ever" and that it "**keeps us alive**": it removes "the pall from our dark spirits" and gives "**quiet breathing**" and "**sleep full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing**". Beauty therefore keeps us healthy and at peace, never depressed. (*The solved booklet circles the third option; the poem supports the fourth.*)

questions.question: Aunt Jennifer's tigers are not afraid of
questions.answer:
**(C)** the men beneath the tree

The poem says of the tigers made on the panel: "**They do not fear the men beneath the tree**." The tigers pace in "sleek and elegant" certainty, unafraid of the men who hunt; it is Aunt Jennifer herself who is afraid, "ringed with ordeals".

questions.question: According to the author, what was garbage for the children?
questions.answer:
**(D)** A wonder

Anees Jung writes that for the ragpicker children of Seemapuri "**garbage to them is gold**" — it is "wrapped in wonder" because a coin or a rupee note may lie hidden in it. Garbage is not a game or a pastime for them; it is a search that sometimes yields treasure.

questions.question: Why did Saheb-e-Alam not go to school?
questions.answer:
**(B)** No money to pay fee

Saheb tells the author "there is no school in my neighbourhood", and the chapter's point is that **poverty**, not indifference, keeps the ragpickers' children out of school: there is no school in the slum and no money in the family to send him to one. Saheb does not choose to stay away — he has nowhere to go.

questions.question: For the last two years, where did all the bad news come from?
questions.answer:
**(A)** The Bulletin Board

Franz notes that "**for the last two years all our bad news had come from there**" — the bulletin board outside the town hall: lost battles, the draft, the orders of the commanding officer. On the day of the last lesson it carried the order from Berlin that only German was to be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine.

questions.question: The wounded soldier belonged to
questions.answer:
**(B)** the U.S. Navy

The wounded man thrown up by the sea is an **American**, a prisoner of war of the **United States Navy** — "a white man" with "a clean-shaven young face", about twenty-five. He is not a Russian, a Briton or a Japanese; that is exactly why Sadao's decision to save him is dangerous.

questions.question: What were Derry and Mr. Lamb victims of?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Physical impairment

Both are **physically impaired**: Derry's face was burnt by acid and one side of it is "eaten away", and Mr. Lamb has **one leg** — a tin leg — after a bomb accident in the war. It is this shared disfigurement that draws the boy into the old man's garden.

questions.question: How did Mr. Lamb help Derry?
options: By giving him a positive outlook on life
questions.answer:
**(D)** By giving him a positive outlook on life

Mr. Lamb's real gift is not apples or sympathy but a **new way of looking**: he tells Derry that the world has more to it than his face — "look at the bees... listen to the wind" — and that people's opinions matter far less than what one thinks of oneself. He changes Derry's self-image from "I'm ugly" to "I'm going to be all right".

questions.question: Zitkala-Sa was being constantly observed by a woman who had
questions.answer:
**(A)** a pale face

In "The Cutting of My Long Hair" Zitkala-Sa remembers being watched "by a **woman with a pale face**" — one of the palefaced staff of the Carlisle school who followed her about and finally held her down while her hair was cut.

questions.question: Where did Douglas go when he was three or four years old, in the story?
questions.answer:
**(C)** California

Douglas writes that he first went to the water at the age of **three or four**, when his father took him to the **beach in California**. The waves knocked him down and buried him in water — the first of the two experiences that gave him his lifelong fear.

questions.question: What does the metaphor 'Rattrap' in the lesson signify?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Human greed and distractions

The peddler's own theory is that the world is a **rattrap**: it offers "baits" — riches, food, shelter, comfort — and "**once the bait is taken, the trap closes**". In the story the metaphor stands for **human greed and the temptations and distractions** that snare a man, as the thirty kronor snare the peddler.

questions.question: What character trait of the prince is revealed when he utters the words 'Let Tigers Beware'?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Pride

The ten-day-old prince's words, "**Let Tigers Beware**", are a boast, and the astrologer's answer takes them up in the same temper. The trait the chapter stresses is the Maharaja's **pride** — a royal self-confidence that becomes an obsession and finally destroys him.

questions.question: Sadao went to America to learn
questions.answer:
**(B)** Surgery and medicine

Dr. Sadao Hoki "had been sent to America to learn **surgery and medicine**", and he came back "a famous surgeon" — he is "the best surgeon in Japan". His skill with the knife is what makes him keep the wounded prisoner alive.

questions.question: Sophie was ....................
questions.answer:
**(D)** a day dreamer

Sophie lives in her fantasies: she invents a meeting with the footballer Danny Casey, describes a boutique she will never own, and half-believes her own story. Jansie, her friend, is the realistic one; Sophie is the **day dreamer**.

questions.question: Which country did Danny Casey play for?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Ireland

Danny Casey is a young **Irish** footballer — the player Sophie "meets" in the alley behind the arcade and the one whose autograph her brother Geoff would love to have. He plays for Ireland, not for any of the other countries listed.

questions.question: Pancake was the brand name of the
questions.answer:
**(B)** make-up material

"Pancake" was the **brand of the thick make-up** used at the Gemini Studios. The chapter's first memory is of the office boy carrying "the make-up material" — the tins of Pancake — to the make-up room.

questions.question: What does the expression 'fiery misery' mean?
questions.answer:
**(D)** discomfort to the actors

Asokamitran describes the make-up room with its "fiery misery" — the **blazing lights and the suffocating heat** under which the actors had to sit and be made up. "Fiery" is literal (the lights) as well as figurative: the misery is the **discomfort of the actors**.

questions.question: What in today's world is our main source of information?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Interviews and interactions

Christopher Silvester's chapter argues that "**the interview**" is the chief source of information in the modern world: "in its highest form" it is "a source of truth", and it is through interviews that we come to know the minds of the people who matter.

questions.question: Who had sent the 'First Day Cover'?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Sam

The **first day cover** — the envelope stamped on the first day of issue of a new stamp, with Galesburg postmarked on it — was sent by **Sam, the psychiatrist**, who had himself gone back to Galesburg of 1894. It is the proof Charley needed that the third level was real.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: What was the name of the southern supercontinent?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Gondwana

Two hundred million years ago all the land was one **supercontinent called Pangaea**, which later split into two — the northern **Laurasia** and the southern **Gondwana**. India, South America, Africa, Antarctica and Australia all came out of Gondwana, which is why the fossils and rocks of Antarctica match theirs.

questions.question: Who insists on being his own master?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Mukesh

**Mukesh** is the one who refuses to accept his inheritance. Where his family has spent generations at the glass furnaces, he says, "I will be a motor mechanic. I will learn to drive a car." The author notes his "**desire to be his own master**" — while Saheb has already become somebody's servant at the tea stall.

questions.question: Who was Sam in 'The Third Level'?
options: A psychiatrist and a friend of Charley
questions.answer:
**(C)** a psychiatrist and a friend of Charley

**Sam** was Charley's **psychiatrist friend**, and it is to him that Charley first tells the story of the third level. Sam calls it "a waking-dream wish to escape" — and then disappears into the very world he had explained away, buying eight hundred dollars' worth of old currency.

questions.question: Who is the author of the lesson 'The Interview'?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Christopher Silvester

"The Interview" is by **Christopher Silvester**, a Cambridge-trained journalist. It was first printed in *The Penguin Book of Interviews*, and it is followed in the chapter by extracts from interviews with Umberto Eco and others.

questions.question: The story 'The Last Lesson' highlights which human tendency?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Procrastination

The heart of the story is Franz's regret: "**I could have learnt my mother tongue**... " — he had always put off learning until tomorrow, "there is plenty of time". M. Hamel himself blames the people of Alsace for putting off their lessons, and the order from Berlin makes the putting-off final.

questions.question:
Read the passage on the Kaziranga centenary celebrations and answer any six of the following:
(a) When did the Kaziranga centenary celebration take place? Who came to attend it?
(b) Who was Nigona Shikari?
(c) What did Lady Curzon visit in Assam?
(d) About what did Nigona Shikari convince Lady Curzon?
(e) What did Nigona complain about the white men?
(f) What was the order issued by the government regarding the rhinos?
(g) What is the meaning of the word 'reserve'?
(h) Give the synonyms of (i) social gathering (ii) make illegal.
questions.answer:
### (a)

**Answer.** The **Kaziranga centenary celebrations began in Assam on 11 February 2005**, and the **five-day fete** was attended by **Nicholas Mosley, the grandson of Lord George Curzon, and his wife Lady Verity**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "The Kaziranga centenary celebrations began in Assam on 11th February, 2005. The five day fete was marked by the presence of Lord George Curzon's grandson, Nicholas Mosley and his wife Lady Verity."

**Why the Curzon connection.** Lord Curzon was the **Viceroy of India from 1898 to 1905**, and it was his wife, Lady Curzon, whose visit to Assam set in motion the creation of the reserve; her grandson's presence a hundred years later closes the circle.

### (b)

**Answer.** Nigona Shikari was the popular name of **Bapiram Hazarika, a local wildlife enthusiast of Assam**. He was the man who "took charge as the mahout of the elephant that was carrying Lady Curzon" and showed her the rhino.

**The passage's own words.**

> "The real story of Kaziranga lies with local wildlife enthusiast Bapiram Hazarika, who was more popularly known as Nigona Shikari."

**His importance.** The passage says that "**it was Nigona Shikari who actually convinced Lady Curzon** about the existence of the great one-horned Indian rhino" — so the park began with a local man's knowledge, not with a government order.

### (c)

**Answer.** On her trip to Assam, Lady Curzon **visited a tea estate**. While she was there she was taken deep into the forest on an elephant, and it was on that ride that the party spotted a rhino.

**The passage's own words.**

> "During a trip to Assam, Lady Curzon visited the tea estate. Nigona Shikari took charge as the Mahout of the elephant that was carrying Lady Curzon. Deep into the forest, they spotted a rhino."

**What followed.** Lady Curzon "asked many questions about rhinos and their habitat", and out of that curiosity came the protection of the forest.

### (d)

**Answer.** He convinced her about the **existence of the great one-horned Indian rhino** in the forest that is today the **Kaziranga National Park**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "It was Nigona Shikari who actually convinced Lady Curzon about the existence of the great one-horned Indian rhino in the forest that we today know as Kaziranga National Park."

**How he did it.** Not by argument but by showing her the animal: he took charge as the mahout of her elephant, led the party "deep into the forest", and there "they spotted a rhino". The sighting was the proof.

### (e)

**Answer.** He complained about the "**indiscriminating killing of the rare animal by white hunters**" — i.e. the reckless, wholesale shooting of the rhinoceros for sport by white hunters, with no regard for how few of the animals were left.

**The passage's own words.**

> "Nigona showed his concern about the indiscriminating killing of the rare animal by white hunters."

**Why it mattered.** His complaint, taken up by Lady Curzon, produced the order prohibiting the hunting of rhinos in Assam — the first legal step towards the national park.

### (f)

**Answer.** The government issued an order **prohibiting the hunting of rhinos in Assam**. Soon afterwards **an area of 57,273.60 acres of forest was declared the Kaziranga Proposed Reserve Forest**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "Later an order was issued to prohibit the hunting of rhinos in Assam. Soon an area of 57,273.60 acres of forest was declared as Kaziranga Proposed Reserve Forest."

**The sequence to remember.** Complaint — order banning the hunt — the declaration of the reserved forest. That is the passage's account of how Kaziranga came into being.

### (g)

**Answer.** A **reserve** is an area of land **set apart and kept for a special purpose** — here, forest land protected by law, where trees and wild animals are preserved and hunting is forbidden.

**In the passage.**

> "...an area of 57,273.60 acres of forest was declared as Kaziranga Proposed **Reserve** Forest."

**Related sense.** The same word means "to keep back for future use" — as in "reserved seats". In the context of wildlife it always means land **protected from ordinary use**, which is why the rhinos were safe once the area was "reserved".

### (h)

**Answer.** (i) Social gathering — **fete**; (ii) Make illegal — **prohibit** (also "ban").

**As used in the passage.**

> "The five day **fete** was marked by the presence of..."

> "...an order was issued to **prohibit** the hunting of rhinos in Assam."

**Note.** Both are the passage's own words; give one word each. "Fete" is a festival or fair, and "prohibit" is to forbid by law.

questions.question: Why was Douglas determined to get over his fear of water? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Douglas was determined because the fear had become a **humiliation and a handicap** that spoilt every pleasure he might have had.

**The reasons.** The memory of being "**paralysed, rigid with terror**" at the bottom of the YMCA pool and of the nine-foot depth "like a great maw" never left him. For years it **spoiled his fishing trips**, took away the joy of **canoeing on the Maine lakes**, and made him afraid even of a small stream. "The fear of the water followed me," he writes, "until I was driven to the decision to overcome it."

**What he did.** He hired an instructor, practised for months — exhaling, kicking, breathing, jumping in with a rope — and then swam alone in the lake, "Lucerne" and the sea, and deliberately went down into the deep water to test himself.

**The result.** The fear was gone: "**All we have to fear is fear itself**", he learnt, and for the first time he felt "a sense of freedom" in the water.

questions.question: Why are the country folks disappointed in the Roadside Stand? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The country folk are disappointed because the **passing cars never stop**. They have built the stand, arranged the "wild berries" and the "golden squash" in "quart" boxes, and polished the "new minted coins" — hoping that the "city money" will come to them.

**Why the hope fails.** The cars go "in a hurry" to the city, and the stand is only a "roadside stand" that nobody sees. The poet says the travellers' cars "**stop for a moment**" only to ask "how far is it to the next town", then move on. The villagers' produce rots, and the money they dream of never arrives.

**The deeper disappointment.** Worse than the loss of profit is the loss of dignity: the villagers are "**pathetically gay**", their faces "strained" with the effort of looking happy for customers who ignore them. The stand becomes a symbol of the gap between the city and the village.

questions.question: What do the parting words of the poet and her smile signify? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The parting words, "**see you soon, amma**", and the smile that accompanies them are a **deliberate cover for fear**.

**What they conceal.** Sitting in the car the poet has seen her mother's face "ashen like that of a corpse" and "pale as a late winter's moon", and she has felt "that old familiar ache" of childhood — the fear of losing her mother. To speak that fear at the airport would be unbearable for both of them. So she smiles and says the cheerful thing, "see you soon", and repeats it.

**What they signify.** The words are **not a promise but a hope and a prayer**, said twice because saying it once is not enough. The smile is a brave mask: the poem's pathos lies in the gap between the cheerful word and the truth the poet has just seen in her mother's face.

**The note on which it ends.** The poem closes on that single line — "and said, see you soon, amma" — so that the farewell is left hanging, hopeful and hopeless at once.

questions.question: What kind of hospitality was received by the peddler when he visited the crofter's house? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The crofter — an **old man living alone** in his cottage on the roadside — gave the peddler a hospitality that the peddler had never known from any other house in the world.

**What he gave him.** He welcomed the stranger at once, "**took him in**", gave him **supper** of porridge and a piece of pork, and let him **sleep** in his room. More than that, he was glad of company: he "was just longing for someone to talk to", and he talked of his cow and showed the peddler the **thirty kronor** he had been paid for the milk.

**Why it matters.** The peddler himself admits that "the old man was generous" and that he "had never been so well off in his life". That generosity is exactly what makes the theft of the thirty kronor soshameful — and it is the memory of a good host that eventually brings the peddler back, a changed man, with the money to return.

questions.question: What work did the office boy do in the Gemini Studio? Why was he disappointed? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The "office boy" — the author himself, Asokamitran — did the **odd jobs of the make-up department** at the Gemini Studios: he carried the **make-up material ("Pancake")** from the store to the make-up room, kept the "fiery misery" of the room supplied, and did whatever small errand the department needed.

**Why he was disappointed.** He had wanted to be a **writer**, and he believed he had it in him. He was, however, "**not a very good writer**" in the eyes of the studio, and his job was to fetch and carry for actors. He watched **Subbu**, the boss's favourite and the studio's most gifted man, and could not help envying his success and his closeness to the boss.

**The irony.** Years later the "office boy" wrote the very account of the studio that we read — the last laugh belongs to the disappointed young man.

questions.question: Who is Hana? How did she help the enemy soldier? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **Hana** is **Dr. Sadao's wife** — a Japanese woman who had met her husband in America, where she had gone to study. She is gentle, obedient and, in the crisis of the story, braver than she knows.

**How she helped the soldier.** When Sadao brings the wounded American home, Hana **washes the man's body**, though she has never touched a white man before, and she **holds the patient down** with the servants' help while Sadao operates. She **feeds him** and keeps the household running while the servants refuse to come into the room. She also understands the danger and helps Sadao decide to hide the man rather than hand him over.

**Her inner struggle.** In the story's central line — "**why are we different from other Japanese?**" — she voices the conflict between duty to the country and duty to a fellow human being, and it is she who makes Sadao's choice possible.

questions.question: What are the different ways in which Mr. Lamb helped Derry to fight his negativity? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Mr. Lamb fights Derry's negativity by **talking, not by pitying**.

**(i) He refuses to look at the face.** He says he has "a tin leg" and Derry a burnt face, and that is all: "you can't see my leg, I can't see your face". **(ii) He turns curiosity into company.** He invites the boy into the garden, shows him the bees, the wind, the weeds and the sun through the trees — "the world is full of things to look at". **(iii) He reverses the boy's self-judgement.** When Derry says nobody will ever love him, Mr. Lamb answers that "**it doesn't matter what they think**", because what matters is what Derry thinks of himself. **(iv) He gives him work to do.** He asks Derry to help him pick apples and to come back — giving him a reason to return.

**The result.** Derry goes back, and returns with the news that he will stay — the beginning of his cure.

questions.question: Who is Mukesh? How is his attitude different from his family? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **Mukesh** is a young bangle-maker of **Firozabad**, the son of a family that has worked for generations in the glass furnaces of the town. He is the boy who takes the author to his home, "a half-built shack", with a roof of "thatch" and a "crumbling wall".

**His attitude.** Everyone around him accepts the bangle trade as fate: his grandmother has "not seen a full meal in her life", his father has gone blind from the dust of the furnaces, and the family believes "it is his kismet". Mukesh **refuses that fate**. He says, "**I will be a motor mechanic. I will learn to drive a car**" — a trade far from the glass furnaces, and one that would take him out of the ghetto.

**Why it matters.** His wish is small and very ordinary, and that is the point: he wants, in the author's words, "to be **his own master**". He is the one hopeful figure in a chapter full of resignation.

questions.question: You found somebody's purse in the school library. Write a notice for the notice board of your school to claim the purse. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**R. K. +2 HIGH SCHOOL, RANCHI**

**NOTICE**

*22 August 2025*

**FOUND: A LADIES' PURSE**

A **brown ladies' purse** was found by me in the **school library**, on a reading table near the window, at about 11 a.m. today.

**Description.** The purse is of brown rexine with a zip that has a small broken tooth at the left edge. It contains some money, a small mirror and a card, but I have deliberately not described the contents in this notice, so that the owner may claim it by identifying them. There is a scratch on the flap in the shape of a "V".

The owner is requested to come to **Class XII-A** during the lunch break or after the last period, and to tell me the colour of the mirror-cover and the amount inside as proof. The purse may also be collected from the **school office**, where I shall deposit it if it is not claimed by **26 August**.

My thanks to the librarian, Mrs. Sinha, who helped me keep it safe.

**Anjali**
Class XII-A
Roll No. 12

**Format points.** Name of the institution, NOTICE, date, a heading, **the object, where and when it was found, identifying marks and the procedure to claim**, and the signature with the class. Never print the contents of the purse in full, or anyone could claim it.

questions.question: You are Anand/Ritika, the cultural secretary of +2 College, Hazaribagh. Write a notice inviting students for writing articles, poems, jokes etc. for the school magazine. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**S. S. +2 COLLEGE, HAZARIBAGH — EDITORIAL BOARD**

**NOTICE**

*10 September 2025*

**CONTRIBUTIONS INVITED FOR THE COLLEGE MAGAZINE**

The Editorial Board invites **original contributions** from all students of the college for the annual magazine, *The Lamp*, to be published in January 2026.

**Sections open.** (1) **Articles** on current affairs, science, social issues and college life — up to 800 words; (2) **Short stories**; (3) **Poems** in Hindi, English or a regional language; (4) **Jokes and light verse**; (5) **Cartoons and sketches** (black ink on white paper); (6) **Book and film reviews**; (7) **Photographs** of college events.

**Conditions.** All work must be **your own**; copied material will be rejected. Write your **name, class, section and roll number** at the top of the page, keep a copy for yourself, and submit the manuscript to the box marked MAGAZINE outside the library, or by email to the address on the library notice board.

**Last date: 15 November 2025.** The editorial board will edit for length and language, and the decision of the board on selection will be final.

**Ritika**
Cultural Secretary

**Format points.** Institution, NOTICE, date, heading, **what is wanted, in what form, the conditions and the deadline**, and signature with the designation — all in the school's own words, with no unnecessary flourishes.

questions.question: Your college organised World Environment Day. Write a report giving details of the programme to be published in your college magazine. You are Radhika/Rohan. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**WORLD ENVIRONMENT DAY OBSERVED WITH A PLANTATION DRIVE**

*By Rohan, Class XII*

**Hazaribagh, 6 June 2025.** World Environment Day was observed at S. S. +2 College, Hazaribagh on 5 June with a **plantation drive, a cleanliness campaign and an inter-house quiz**, the whole programme running from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m.

**The morning.** The Principal, Dr. R. P. Verma, planted a **neem sapling** in the college lawn and spoke for ten minutes on the theme of the year, reminding the students that "a tree planted today is shade for a generation". Two hundred saplings — neem, gulmohar, peepal and jamun — were then planted by students along the boundary wall and in the vacant plot behind the science block.

**The campaign.** From 10 a.m. groups of twenty students, each with a teacher in charge, cleaned the college ground, the canteen area and the road outside the gate. Four **dustbins** donated by the local municipality were installed at the gate.

**The quiz.** An inter-house environment quiz was held in the auditorium at 11.30 a.m.; the Green House won, with Blue House second.

**The pledge.** The programme ended with an **environment pledge** administered to the whole assembly, promising to reduce the use of plastic and to keep the campus green. The Principal announced that the saplings would be watered by the students of each class in rotation.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, place and date, the **sequence and timing of the programme**, the numbers and names, the dignitary's words, and the concluding pledge — all in the past tense, without personal opinion.

questions.question: You witnessed a Sports Day programme. Write a report giving details of the programme. You are the reporter to the Hindustan Times. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**SPORTS DAY AT DAV SCHOOL: CITY ATHLETE SETS NEW MEET RECORD**

*By a Staff Reporter*

**Ranchi, 18 November 2025.** The annual **Sports Day** of DAV Public School, Doranda, was held on 17 November on the school ground, with more than six hundred students taking part in twenty-four events before a crowd of parents and teachers.

**The inauguration.** The meet was declared open at 8.30 a.m. by the **Deputy Commissioner, Ranchi**, who took the salute at a march past of the four school houses. The Principal, Mrs. A. K. Nair, welcomed the guests; the school band played as the houses marched in their colours.

**The events.** The morning was given to the track events — 100 m, 200 m, 400 m, relay and hurdles — and the afternoon to the field events: long jump, high jump, shot put, javelin and discus throw. The highlight was the **under-17 boys' 200 m**, in which **Rohit Oraon of Blue House** broke the meet record of 2009 with a time of **23.4 seconds**. In the girls' section, **Sneha Kumari of Green House** won the 100 m and the long jump.

**The closing.** The District Sports Officer gave away the prizes. Green House won the overall championship with 184 points. The meet ended with a **march past and the National Anthem** at 5 p.m. The Principal announced that the school would send its winners to the district-level meet in December.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, place and date, the **programme in order, the guests, the events and the results, and the closing**, all in the past tense.

questions.question: Write a letter to the editor focusing on the disposal of garbage in your area. You are Seema/Suraj of Ashok Nagar, Ranchi. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Ashok Nagar**
**Ranchi**
**4 July 2025**

The Editor
*The Telegraph*
Ranchi

**Subject: Mounting garbage and the failure of garbage disposal in Ashok Nagar**

Sir

Through the columns of your esteemed daily I wish to draw the attention of the civic authorities to the **disposal of garbage in Ashok Nagar**, which has become a public hazard.

**The situation.** The two bins at the corner of the lane have not been emptied for more than a week, and the waste now lies on the road and in the drain that runs beside it. The sweepers of the ward have not come for ten days; the vans that were supposed to collect from door to door have stopped after the first fortnight. In the evenings the lane smells so badly that the windows cannot be opened, and stray dogs and cattle scatter the waste over the road.

**The consequences.** Mosquitoes and flies breed in the standing water of the choked drain, and at least nine families in the lane have had fever this month. Children play beside the pile. Shopkeepers have begun to burn their waste, which fills the whole colony with a foul smoke.

**The remedy.** I request the Municipal Commissioner to **send the collection van on a fixed schedule**, to repair or replace the two bins, to **clear the choked drain** before the monsoon, and to fine those who dump waste at the corner instead of in the bin. A simple notice with the day and hour of collection in each lane would prevent half the trouble.

Yours faithfully
**Seema**

**Format points.** Sender's address and date, addressee, subject, the **problem with specific facts and consequences**, a set of practical remedies, and the formal close.

questions.question: Recently your school organised a skit competition on the occasion of Gandhi Jayanti. Write a letter to your friend giving the details of your experience. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**R. K. +2 High School**
**Ranchi**
**4 October 2025**

My dear Aditya

I must tell you about our **Gandhi Jayanti skit competition** — the best thing that has happened at school this year.

The whole school gathered in the assembly hall at 9 a.m. on 2 October, and the hall was decorated with white khadi and marigold. There were seven teams, one from each class, and every team had ten minutes. Our class chose the **Champaran episode** — Gandhi's visit to the indigo sharecroppers — and I was given the role of Rajkumar Shukla. I had to follow "Gandhiji" about the stage, refusing to leave him alone, and the audience laughed at exactly the right moment, which I had not expected at all.

But the best act was by Class XI: they showed the **Dandi March**, with the boys walking in a line behind a boy holding a staff, and one of them speaking the salt-law sentence with such conviction that the hall went completely silent. The judges, two teachers and our old Sanskrit teacher, gave them the first prize; our class came third, which was more than we deserved.

What struck me most was that none of us had to be told to stay quiet during the performances. On an ordinary morning we chatter through the announcements; that morning nobody did.

Write and tell me what your school did on 2 October.

Your loving friend
**Rohan**

**Format points.** Address and date, familiar salutation, **the details the question asks for** — the occasion, the teams, the acts, the result — and a personal reflection, within 250 words.
